name: Josh
bio:
I’ve always wanted to see what was underneath the surface. As a kid, that meant opening up toys, electronics, or anything mechanical I could get my hands on just to see how the pieces worked together. I also loved building things, whether it was with Legos, cardboard, or whatever materials I could find.

Before I got my first job, I started picking up free, non-running lawn mowers from Facebook Marketplace, fixing them, and selling them to make some side cash. Not long after that, I got my first 3D printer, which gave me a whole new way to design and make things myself. During high school, my dad got a welder, and I started learning how to fabricate things out of metal, including projects like a custom strut bar. I later spent two summers working as a mechanic at a local shop, where I gained more hands on experience troubleshooting and repairing vehicles.

I’m now a mechanical engineering student at Washington State University, where I’ve become familiar with CAD and enjoy using it to bring my ideas to life. I also manage a composite manufacturing studio sponsored by Janicki Industries, which has given me the opportunity to dive deep into the world of composite manufacturing. Studying engineering has allowed me to keep building on the same curiosity and love for designing and making things that has been with me from the start.
personal: Me (left) with Adam Schultz, my boss at Schultz & Sons Automotive, during the summer of 2025.

hobbies.title: Snowboarding
hobbies.text: There's nothing else that feels like being on the mountains on a fresh snowy day. When I'm snowboarding, I feel free. Everything else fades away, and the only thing that matters is being outside and riding fast.

hobbies.title: Backpacking
hobbies.text: Packing a backpack with everything I need for a few days and heading into the mountains is something I really enjoy. I like being able to get away for a while, explore new places, and camp wherever I end up.

hobbies.title: Fishing
hobbies.text: Fishing is something I enjoy because it gives me a reason to spend time outside and slow things down for a bit. I like finding new spots, being out by the water, and the adrenaline of feeling a fish hit the line.

projects.title: 1989 Toyota Pickup
projects.description: Swapping the engine, wiring harness, and ECU from a 1999 Toyota 4Runner into my 1989 Toyota pickup.
projects.coverText:
A new heart.
An old Toyota.

items.alt: The day I got my 1989 Toyota pickup.
My dogs sitting in the bed of my Toyota pickup.

sections.text: The day that I got my truck. I drove to Oregon to get it, and the drive back was truly an experience. I also took a picture of my dogs in my truck, just like how my dad did when he got his truck.

sections.alt: Blank placeholder for the oil discovery.
sections.text: I changed the oil and found coolant mixed in with it, which pointed to a blown head gasket. I was pretty pissed when I realized the seller had screwed me over.

items.alt: Working on the truck during the day during the head gasket repair.
Working on the truck at night during the head gasket repair.

sections.text: I worked day and night on the head gasket. At that point, this was the most complicated thing I had ever done in my life.

items.alt: Top of the pistons showing heavy carbon buildup.

sections.text: The tops of the pistons had tons of carbon buildup, so I cleaned them up.
Finally, I turned the key and heard the beautiful sound of my engine that I rebuilt, running.

sections.alt: Later engine swap work on the Toyota pickup.

projects.title: Carbon Fiber Coaster
projects.description: For training in the Janicki Industries-sponsored Composites Studio, we make forged-carbon WSU Cougar coasters.

items.alt: Resin applied to the coaster mold.
Chopped carbon fiber added to the mold.

sections.text: First, you prepare the molds by cleaning them and applying mold release to the surfaces. Then you wet the surface with resin and add a small layer of chopped carbon fiber.

items.alt: Stippling resin into the chopped carbon fiber.
Carbon fiber saturated with resin in the mold.
Compressing the mold with bolts and clamps.

sections.text: Then, with a paintbrush, you slowly saturate the fibers by stippling until they are fully wet out. Repeat until all of the measured carbon fiber is used. Then you compress the mold using bolts and clamps.

items.alt: Close-up of a cured WSU Cougar coaster.

sections.text: I let them cure according to the resin manufacturer’s instructions, then get them out (easier said than done). You can see the coasters aren’t perfect. There are visible voids, and the logo is primarily resin where the fibers weren’t able to fit and bridging occurred.

sections.alt: Photo placeholder for the first furnace design.
sections.text: I wanted to make my own billet aluminum stock by melting aluminum cans. My first design used a propane tank with a tube cut and welded into the tank at a tangent angle, an air mattress inflator for airflow, and a fire extinguisher cut in half to use as a crucible.
